actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-easton}{cited=Easton1970}{Easton's theorem on regular cardinals}
Let \(F\) be a definable class function from the infinite regular cardinals to
cardinals such that
\(\kappa<\lambda\) implies \(F(\kappa)\leq F(\lambda)\), and
\(\operatorname{cf}(F(\kappa))>\kappa\) for every regular \(\kappa\).
Starting from a ground model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}+\mathsf{GCH}\) carrying such an
\(F\), Easton's forcing yields a cofinality-preserving generic extension in
which \(2^\kappa=F(\kappa)\) at every infinite regular cardinal \(\kappa\).
Thus monotonicity and K\"onig's cofinality condition are, relative to the
existence of the stated ground model, the only restrictions on the continuum
function at regular cardinals.  The theorem does not prescribe exponentiation
at singular cardinals and is a relative-consistency result, not a theorem that
\(\mathsf{ZFC}\) chooses one such function in the ground universe.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-measurable-ultrapower}{cited=Kanamori2003}{Measurability and the universe ultrapower}
If \(\mathcal U\) is a nonprincipal \(\kappa\)-complete ultrafilter on
\(\kappa\), the class ultrapower \(\operatorname{Ult}(V,\mathcal U)\) is well
founded.  Its transitive
collapse yields a nontrivial elementary embedding
\[
  j_{\mathcal U}:V\longrightarrow M
  \qquad\text{with}\qquad
  \operatorname{crit}(j_{\mathcal U})=\kappa.
\]
Conversely, such an embedding with critical point \(\kappa\) recovers a
nonprincipal \(\kappa\)-complete ultrafilter by
\[
  \mathcal U=\{X\subseteq\kappa:\kappa\in j(X)\}.
\]
The complete class-ultrapower construction is cited; this statement is not a
compressed local proof of its coding and well-foundedness obligations.
The ultrapower role is historically attached to \cite{Keisler1962}; the
modern large-cardinal formulation is \cite{Kanamori2003}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-shoenfield-absoluteness}{cited=Moschovakis2009}{Shoenfield absoluteness}
Let \(M\subseteq N\) be transitive models of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) with the same
ordinals, and let the real parameter \(a\) belong to \(M\).  Then \(M\) and
\(N\) agree on every boldface \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2(a)\) sentence and,
by complementation, on every boldface \(\boldsymbol\Pi^1_2(a)\) sentence.
The hypotheses do not reduce to agreement about \(\omega\), and the theorem
does not assert absoluteness for all higher projective levels.
The original theorem is \cite{Shoenfield1961}; the displayed modern
second-order formulation is supported by \cite{Moschovakis2009}.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-delta-system}{proved=annex:p6.comb.1}{Delta-system lemma}
In \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), every uncountable family of finite sets has an
uncountable subfamily that is a delta system with a finite root.  No
generalization to families of sets of size below an arbitrary \(\kappa\) is
asserted here; such versions require additional hypotheses
\cite{Shanin1946,Jech2003}.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p6.comb.1}{thm:p06-delta-system}{Delta-system lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal A\) be an uncountable family of finite sets.  Since
\[
  \mathcal A=\bigcup_{n<\omega}
  \{a\in\mathcal A:\abs a=n\}
\]
and a countable union of countable sets is countable in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\),
there are an \(n<\omega\) and an uncountable
\(\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal A\) consisting of \(n\)-element sets.

We prove the fixed-size assertion by induction on \(n\).  The case \(n=0\)
is vacuous.  Suppose it holds for \(n\), and let \(\mathcal A_0\) be an
uncountable family of \((n+1)\)-element sets.  If \(\mathcal A_0\) has an
uncountable pairwise-disjoint subfamily, that subfamily is a
delta system with root \(\varnothing\).

Otherwise, use Zorn's lemma to choose a maximal pairwise-disjoint
\(\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal A_0\).  The case assumption makes
\(\mathcal E\) countable, so \(Y=\bigcup\mathcal E\) is countable.
Maximality ensures that every \(a\in\mathcal A_0\) meets \(Y\).  Hence
\[
  \mathcal A_0=
  \bigcup_{x\in Y}\{a\in\mathcal A_0:x\in a\}.
\]
Some \(x\in Y\) therefore belongs to uncountably many members; call that
subfamily \(\mathcal A_x\).  The map
\(a\mapsto a\setminus\{x\}\) is injective on \(\mathcal A_x\), and its
range is an uncountable family of \(n\)-element sets.  By induction it has an
uncountable delta-system subfamily with root \(R_\ast\).  Restoring \(x\)
gives an uncountable delta-system subfamily of \(\mathcal A_x\) with root
\(R_\ast\cup\{x\}\).  This completes the induction.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p6.comb.2}{thm:p06-add-ccc}{The Cohen poset is ccc}
\begin{proof}
Let \(A\) be an uncountable family of finite conditions.  The
set \(\{\dom(p):p\in A\}\) is uncountable: a fixed finite domain \(d\)
supports only \(2^{\abs d}\) binary conditions.  Apply the delta-system
lemma to these domains, and choose one condition over each domain in the
resulting uncountable subfamily.  This gives an uncountable
\(A'\subseteq A\) whose domains have a common root \(d_\ast\).  Only finitely
many binary functions on \(d_\ast\) exist, so an uncountable
\(A''\subseteq A'\) has one fixed restriction to \(d_\ast\).  Any two members
of \(A''\) agree on their overlap and their union is
a common strengthening.  Thus no uncountable \(A\) is an antichain.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-infinite-ramsey}{cited=Ramsey1930}{Infinite Ramsey theorem}
For every positive finite \(\ell\) and every positive finite \(k\),
\[
  \omega\longrightarrow(\omega)^\ell_k.
\]
Equivalently, every finite coloring of the \(\ell\)-element subsets of
\(\omega\) has an infinite homogeneous set \cite{Ramsey1930}.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p06-boolean-valued-universe}{Boolean-valued universe}
Let \(\mathbb B\) be a complete Boolean algebra, meaning that every subset of
\(\mathbb B\) has a join and a meet.  Write
\(b^{\complement_{\mathbb B}}\), \(b\wedge_{\mathbb B}c\), and
\(b\vee_{\mathbb B}c\) for Boolean complement, meet, and join; these
subscripts distinguish Boolean-algebra operations from the globally
registered object-language connectives.  Define recursively
\[
  V^{\mathbb B}_\alpha
  \defeq\left\{\mathbf u:
      \begin{array}{l}
      \mathbf u\text{ is a function},\quad
      \operatorname{ran}(\mathbf u)\subseteq\mathbb B,\\
      \dom(\mathbf u)\subseteq
        \displaystyle\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}V^{\mathbb B}_\beta
      \end{array}\right\}.
\]
Put
\[
  V^{\mathbb B}\defeq
  \bigcup_{\alpha\in\operatorname{Ord}}V^{\mathbb B}_\alpha.
\]
The members of \(V^{\mathbb B}\) are \(\mathbb B\)-names.  The Boolean truth
map \(\operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}\) is the simultaneous recursion
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\mathbf u\in\mathbf v)
   &\defeq\mathop{\bigvee}\nolimits^{\mathbb B}_{\mathbf w\in\dom(\mathbf v)}
       \mathbf v(\mathbf w)\wedge_{\mathbb B}
       \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\mathbf u=\mathbf w),\\
 \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\mathbf u=\mathbf v)
   &\defeq\mathop{\bigwedge}\nolimits^{\mathbb B}_{\mathbf w\in\dom(\mathbf u)}
       \bigl(\mathbf u(\mathbf w)^{\complement_{\mathbb B}}\vee_{\mathbb B}
             \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\mathbf w\in\mathbf v)\bigr)\\
   &\quad\wedge_{\mathbb B}
     \mathop{\bigwedge}\nolimits^{\mathbb B}_{\mathbf w\in\dom(\mathbf v)}
       \bigl(\mathbf v(\mathbf w)^{\complement_{\mathbb B}}\vee_{\mathbb B}
             \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\mathbf w\in\mathbf u)\bigr),\\
 \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\neg\varphi)
   &\defeq
     \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\varphi)^{\complement_{\mathbb B}},\\
 \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\varphi\wedge\psi)
   &\defeq\operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\varphi)\wedge_{\mathbb B}
       \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\psi),\\
 \operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}(\exists x\,\varphi(x,\bar{\mathbf v}))
   &\defeq\mathop{\bigvee}\nolimits^{\mathbb B}
       S_{\varphi,\bar{\mathbf v}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
At the existential step of the simultaneous recursion, define
\[
 S_{\varphi,\bar{\mathbf v}}
 \defeq
 \left\{b\in\mathbb B:
   \exists\mathbf u\in V^{\mathbb B}\,
   b=\operatorname{Bool}_{\mathbb B}
      (\varphi(\mathbf u,\bar{\mathbf v}))\right\}.
\]
This is a set by Separation because it is a subclass of the set
\(\mathbb B\); completeness of \(\mathbb B\) therefore supplies the displayed
join.  Equivalently one may rank-bound the witness names and prove that the
value stabilizes above the parameter ranks.  The class
\(V^{\mathbb B}\) is never used as a primitive proper-class index for a
Boolean join \cite{ScottSolovay1967,Bell2005}.

The remaining connectives and \(\forall\) are defined from these.  Completeness
of \(\mathbb B\) is needed for the displayed set-indexed joins and meets.  This map has
Boolean-algebra values and is neither the two-valued satisfaction relation nor
the forcing relation of Chapter~\ref{ch:constructibility-forcing}.  Unlike
a \(\mathbb P\)-name, a \(\mathbb B\)-name is a Boolean-valued function on
earlier names, not a set of name--condition pairs; this distinction is exactly
what the generic-quotient theorem uses.
\index{Boolean-valued model!truth map}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-nice-name-counting}{proved=annex:p6.force.10}{Nice-name reduction and counting}
Under Convention~\ref{def:p06-ccc-forcing-standing}, assume \(M\) regards
\(\mathbb P\) as ccc.  If \(p\in\mathbb P\) and
\(p\forces\nu\subseteq\check\omega\), then some nice
\(\mathbb P\)-name \(\zeta\) satisfies \(p\forces\nu=\zeta\).
Consequently, if \(\mathbb P\) is infinite and
\(\lambda=(\abs{\mathbb P}^{\aleph_0})^M\), then
\[
  M[G]\entails 2^{\aleph_0}\leq\lambda.
\]
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p6.force.9}{thm:p06-ccc-preservation}{Cardinal and cofinality preservation by ccc forcing}
\begin{proof}
Work in \(M\), using Choice.  First note that if \(D\in M\) is dense below
some \(d\in G\), then
\[
  D\cup\{q\in\mathbb P:q\text{ is incompatible with }d\}
\]
is a globally dense member of \(M\).  Genericity and \(d\in G\) therefore
give \(G\cap D\neq\varnothing\).

If \(M[G]\) collapsed an uncountable
\(M\)-cardinal \(\kappa\), there would be an ordinal
\(\lambda<\kappa\), a surjection \(f:\lambda\to\kappa\) in \(M[G]\), a
name \(\nu_f\in M\) with \(\nu_f^G=f\), and \(p\in G\) such that
\(p\forces \nu_f:\check\lambda\twoheadrightarrow\check\kappa\).  For each
\(\alpha<\lambda\), choose below \(p\) a maximal antichain deciding
\(\nu_f(\check\alpha)\).  The ccc makes it countable; if \(X_\alpha\) is its set
of possible values, the downward closure of that antichain is dense below
\(p\).  The observation above shows that the interpreted map satisfies
\[
  \operatorname{ran}(f)\subseteq
  \bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}X_\alpha.
\]
In \(M\), the union has size at
most \(\max((\abs\lambda)^M,\aleph_0)<\kappa\), impossible.  The finite cardinals
and \(\omega\) are absolute because the extension has the same ordinals.

Now let \(\mu=\operatorname{cf}^{M}(\delta)\).  A ground-model cofinal map
of type \(\mu\) remains cofinal because the ordinals and their order are
unchanged, so cofinality cannot increase.  If a cofinal map in \(M[G]\) had
infinite domain ordinal \(\lambda<\mu\), choose a name and a condition in
\(G\) forcing this, and repeat the deciding-antichain construction below that
condition.  Since \(\mu\) is regular, the resulting union of possible values
has size \(\max((\abs\lambda)^M,\aleph_0)<\mu\) in \(M\), hence is bounded in
\(\delta\), contradicting cofinality.  A finite range is bounded in every
limit ordinal, so ground cofinality \(\omega\) cannot drop to a finite value;
successor and zero cofinalities are fixed by the unchanged ordinals.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p6.force.10}{thm:p06-nice-name-counting}{Nice-name reduction and counting}
\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\forces\nu\subseteq\check\omega\).  For each \(n<\omega\), choose
below \(p\) a maximal antichain \(A_n\) among conditions forcing
\(\check n\in\nu\).  Put
\[
  \zeta=\bigcup_{n<\omega}
  \{\langle\check n,a\rangle:a\in A_n\}.
\]
For any generic \(H\ni p\), a member of \(A_n\cap H\) forces
\(n\in\zeta^H\cap\nu^H\).  Conversely, if \(n\in\nu^H\), the truth lemma
gives \(q\in H\) forcing \(\check n\in\nu\).  Directedness supplies
\(d\in H\) with \(d\leq p,q\), which still forces membership.  Maximality
makes the common extensions of \(d\) with members of \(A_n\) dense below
\(d\).  Adjoining every condition incompatible with \(d\) makes this set a
globally dense member of \(M\).  Since \(d\in H\), genericity cannot meet the
incompatible part, so it supplies a common extension in \(H\); upward closure
then puts the corresponding member of \(A_n\) in \(H\).  Hence
\(n\in\zeta^H\).  Thus
\(p\) semantically forces \(\nu=\zeta\), and the forcing theorem yields
\(p\forces\nu=\zeta\).

Under ccc each \(A_n\) is countable.  There are at most
\(\lambda=(\abs{\mathbb P}^{\aleph_0})^M\) countable subsets of
\(\mathbb P\) in \(M\), and a countable sequence of them has the same bound.
For any \(x\subseteq\omega\) in \(M[G]\), choose \(\nu\in M\) with
\(x=\nu^G\).  The truth lemma supplies \(p\in G\) forcing
\(\nu\subseteq\check\omega\), so the local result gives a nice \(\zeta\)
with \(x=\zeta^G\).  Thus the nice names cover all reals; ccc preservation
keeps \(\lambda\) a cardinal, proving the bound.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-suslin}{cited=Kechris1995}{Suslin's theorem}
Let \(X\) be Polish and \(A\subseteq X\).  Then
\[
  A\in\operatorname{Bor}(X)
  \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
  A\in
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1}_{1}(X)
  \cap
  \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{1}_{1}(X).
\]
Equivalently,
\(\operatorname{Bor}(X)=\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1}_{1}(X)\).
The historical source is \cite{Suslin1917}; the status citation supports the
modern Polish-space formulation.

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p06-martin-steel}{cited=MartinSteel1989}{Martin--Steel calibration}
Let \(n\geq1\).  If there are \(n\) Woodin cardinals below a measurable
cardinal, then games whose payoffs lie in
\(\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{1}_{n+1}\), and games with complementary
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1}_{n+1}\) payoffs, are determined.  Consequently, if
for every positive integer \(n\) there are \(n\) Woodin cardinals below a
measurable cardinal---for example, if infinitely many Woodin cardinals lie
below one measurable cardinal---then \(\mathsf{PD}\) holds.

This is a sufficient large-cardinal hypothesis.  The theorem as stated does
not assert an equivalence, does not assert that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) proves the
required cardinals exist, and does not identify \(\mathsf{PD}\) with
\(\mathsf{AD}\).
\end{hbtheorem}

For every finite propositional sequent \(\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta\), canonical
\(\mathsf{LK}\) derives the sequent exactly when it is valid under every
valuation.  For every finite equality-free first-order sequent, the analogous
equivalence holds under every structure and assignment, assuming the Axiom of

countable-language completeness route needs no Choice.  Empty antecedents and
empty succedents are included, and no cut-free-completeness claim is made.

\begin{hblemma}{thm:p07-maehara-partition}{proved=annex:p7.interp.1}{Maehara's partition lemma}
Every partition of the endsequent of a cut-free equality-free derivation in
the purely relational restriction of \(\mathsf{LK}_{\mathrm d}\) has a partition interpolant in the
sense of Definition~\ref{def:p07-partition-interpolant}.  In particular, if
the four endsequent contexts contain only sentences, the interpolant is a
sentence.
\end{hblemma}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p7.interp.2}{thm:p07-relational-cut-free-completeness}{Relational soundness and cut-free completeness}
\begin{proof}
Use exactly the rules of \texttt{sheet:lk-defneg}, with variables as the
only terms and \(\neg A\) expanded as \(A\to\bot\).

\paragraph{Soundness.}
Call a structure and assignment a counterexample to
\(\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta\) when every member of \(\Gamma\) is true
and every member of \(\Delta\) is false.
Identity and \(\bot L\) have no counterexamples.
Weakening can only add a required true antecedent or false succedent,
and contraction removes repeated copies of one unchanged truth condition.
Consequently a counterexample to the conclusion of a structural rule
is a counterexample to its premise.

For \(\land L\), a true conjunction makes both premise conjuncts true;
for \(\lor R\), a false disjunction makes both disjuncts false.
A false implication in \(\to R\) has a true antecedent and false
consequent.  These observations give a counterexample to the unique
premise in each case.
For \(\land R\), a false principal conjunction has a false conjunct,
selecting a false premise.  For \(\lor L\), a true principal disjunction
has a true disjunct, again selecting a false premise.
For split-context \(\to L\), a true principal \(A\to B\) has either
false \(A\) or true \(B\).  The former falsifies the premise with
\(A\) in its succedent, and the latter falsifies the premise with
\(B\) in its antecedent.  The counterexample already satisfies both
split antecedent contexts and falsifies both split succedent contexts.

For \(\forall L\), truth of \(\forall xA\) gives truth of the displayed
instance \(A[a/x]\).  For \(\exists R\), falsity of \(\exists xA\)
gives falsity of every such instance.  Both use the substitution lemma.
If the conclusion of \(\forall R\) is false, choose a value falsifying
its quantified matrix and assign it to the fresh eigenvariable.
The other conclusion formulas keep their truth values by freshness,
so the premise is false.  If the conclusion of \(\exists L\) is false,
choose a witnessing value for its true existential antecedent and make
the same fresh-variable assignment; the premise is false.
Finally, a counterexample to a Cut conclusion falsifies the first
premise when the cut formula is false, and the second when it is true.
The same argument handles all displayed copies in Mix.
Induction up a derivation proves soundness.

\paragraph{Persistent backward steps.}
For completeness it suffices to consider the finite predicate signature
occurring in the endsequent.  A model of that signature can interpret
every unused predicate as empty.  Fix a countably infinite set
\(V=\{v_0,v_1,\ldots\}\) of variables, containing all variables of the
endsequent.
In this proof, \emph{unprovable} means having no derivation without Cut or Mix.
Suppose the endsequent is unprovable.
We construct larger finite antecedent and succedent sets, retaining all
formulas already present.  Using sets during this construction is harmless:
the registered weakening and contraction rules convert them to and from
the corresponding finite multiset contexts.

The following backward steps add the indicated formulas.  A vertical
choice denotes two alternative successors.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
 \text{side}&\text{principal formula}&\text{added formulas}\\ \hline
 \Gamma&A\land B&A,B\text{ in }\Gamma\\
 \Delta&A\lor B&A,B\text{ in }\Delta\\
 \Delta&A\to B&A\text{ in }\Gamma,\ B\text{ in }\Delta\\
 \Gamma&A\lor B&A\text{ in }\Gamma\ \mid\ B\text{ in }\Gamma\\
 \Delta&A\land B&A\text{ in }\Delta\ \mid\ B\text{ in }\Delta\\
 \Gamma&A\to B&A\text{ in }\Delta\ \mid\ B\text{ in }\Gamma\\
 \Gamma&\forall xA&A[a/x]\text{ in }\Gamma,\quad a\in V\\
 \Delta&\exists xA&A[a/x]\text{ in }\Delta,\quad a\in V\\
 \Gamma&\exists xA&A[b/x]\text{ in }\Gamma,\quad b\text{ fresh}\\
 \Delta&\forall xA&A[b/x]\text{ in }\Delta,\quad b\text{ fresh}
\end{array}
\]
All substitutions are capture avoiding.
For either eigenvariable step, choose \(b\) absent from the entire
current sequent and from the earlier eigenvariable choices.
Only finitely many variables are excluded at a finite stage.

If every successor of one of these steps were provable, the current
sequent would be provable.  To see this, apply the corresponding
registered logical rule to the successor derivation or derivations,
then contract the extra copy of the retained principal formula.
For \(\forall L\) and \(\exists R\), the chosen \(a\) is an allowed
term, so the same simulation applies to every \(a\in V\).
For the two eigenvariable rules, the displayed freshness condition
is exactly the one required by the forward inference.
For split \(\to L\), the two successor derivations have the whole
current context.  Applying \(\to L\) duplicates that context on both
sides; contract these copies and the repeated principal implication.
No Cut or Mix is used in any of these simulations.
An identity overlap, or \(\bot\) in the antecedent, would also give
an immediate proof by identity and weakening, or by \(\bot L\).
Thus an unprovable current sequent has no such closure and has at
least one unprovable successor at every applicable step.

\paragraph{Fair saturation.}
There are countably many formulas in the finite predicate signature
over \(V\).  Enumerate the possible expansion tasks, including a separate
task for every pair consisting of a \(\forall\)-antecedent or
\(\exists\)-succedent formula and a variable \(a\in V\).
In pass \(s\), inspect the first \(s\) tasks.  Perform a task when
its principal formula is present and the task has not already been
performed.  For a branching task, choose an unprovable successor;
for an eigenvariable task, record its fresh witness and perform it
once.  Every pass is finite.  An inapplicable task remains available
in later passes, and a pass with no applicable tasks leaves the
sequent unchanged.

This is a classical existence construction: it does not presume an
algorithm deciding whether a sequent is unprovable.  There are at
most two successor choices, and the preceding paragraph proves that
an unprovable one exists.  Recursion, selecting the first such choice
in a fixed order, gives an increasing sequence
\((\Gamma_s,\Delta_s)\) of finite unprovable sequents.
Let
\[
 \Gamma_\infty=\bigcup_s\Gamma_s,\qquad
 \Delta_\infty=\bigcup_s\Delta_s.
\]
Every task for a formula that enters either union is inspected in
every sufficiently late pass, so it is eventually performed.
In particular, every \(\forall\)-antecedent and
\(\exists\)-succedent receives its instance for \emph{every} variable
in \(V\), including variables not free in the initial sequent.
Each \(\exists\)-antecedent and \(\forall\)-succedent has a witnessing
instance in the required union.  All six propositional saturation
conditions in the table hold.
No formula belongs to both unions: its two occurrences would already
coexist in one finite stage and close that sequent.
Also \(\bot\notin\Gamma_\infty\).

\paragraph{The countermodel.}
Take domain \(V\), and let the assignment \(s_0\) send each variable
to itself.  For each \(m\)-ary predicate \(P\), define
\[
 P^{\mathcal M}
   =\{(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in V^m:
                    P(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in\Gamma_\infty\}.
\]
When \(m=0\), this gives the corresponding truth value by membership
of the nullary atom.  The domain is nonempty.
We prove simultaneously, by formula complexity, that every formula
in \(\Gamma_\infty\) is true at \((\mathcal M,s_0)\) and every
formula in \(\Delta_\infty\) is false there.

The atomic claims follow from the definition of the relations and
the absence of an overlap.  Bottom is always false and is absent
from the antecedent.  For an antecedent conjunction, both conjuncts
are present in \(\Gamma_\infty\); for a succedent conjunction, one
conjunct is present in \(\Delta_\infty\).  The two disjunction cases
are dual.  An antecedent implication has either its antecedent in
\(\Delta_\infty\) or its consequent in \(\Gamma_\infty\), making it
true.  A succedent implication has its antecedent in \(\Gamma_\infty\)
and consequent in \(\Delta_\infty\), making it false.

For \(\forall xA\in\Gamma_\infty\), every \(A[a/x]\), \(a\in V\),
belongs to \(\Gamma_\infty\).  The induction hypothesis and the
substitution lemma give truth of \(A\) under every value for \(x\),
since every domain element is one of these variables.
For \(\exists xA\in\Delta_\infty\), the same argument with every
instance in \(\Delta_\infty\) makes the existential false.
For \(\exists xA\in\Gamma_\infty\), its recorded witness instance
is true by induction, making the existential true.
For \(\forall xA\in\Delta_\infty\), its recorded witness instance
is false, making the universal false.
Substitution of a variable changes no logical complexity, so every
instance used here lies within the induction hypothesis.

The resulting structure and assignment falsify the original sequent.
Thus a valid finite sequent cannot be unprovable.  Together with
soundness, this proves the stated equivalence.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p7.interp.3}{thm:craig-interpolation}{Craig interpolation}
\begin{proof}
\paragraph{The relational case.}
Let \(A,B\) be equality-free purely relational sentences with
\(\models A\to B\).
Theorem~\ref{thm:p07-relational-cut-free-completeness} supplies a
cut-free derivation of \(A\Rightarrow B\).
Put \(A\) in the first antecedent part and \(B\) in the second
succedent part of its partition.
Theorem~\ref{thm:p07-maehara-partition} supplies a sentence \(J\)
in the common predicate vocabulary, with derivations of
\(A\Rightarrow J\) and \(J\Rightarrow B\).
Soundness gives \(\models A\to J\) and \(\models J\to B\).
This establishes the relational case, including an empty common
predicate vocabulary.

\paragraph{A finite relational signature for each side.}
Now let \(A,B\) be arbitrary first-order sentences with
\(\models A\to B\).
Write \(\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2\) for their respective finite sets of
nonlogical symbols, with arities retained.
Only the union of these finite signatures is needed.
Every nonempty structure in that union extends to any unused
original symbols by assigning empty predicates and constant-valued
functions at one fixed element.

Introduce one fresh binary predicate \(E\).
For every \(m\)-ary function symbol \(f\), introduce a distinct
\((m+1)\)-ary predicate \(G_f\).  Thus a constant \(c\), regarded
as a function of arity zero, has a unary predicate \(G_c\).
Keep original predicate symbols unchanged.
The translated language is purely relational and has no logical
equality, functions, or constants.

For a finite signature \(\Sigma\), let \(\operatorname{Ax}_\Sigma\)
be the conjunction of the following finite set of relational sentences.
First require \(E\) to be an equivalence relation:
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \forall x\,E(x,x),\\
 \forall x\,y\,(E(x,y)\to E(y,x)),\\
 \forall x\,y\,z\,
       ((E(x,y)\land E(y,z))\to E(x,z)).
\end{gathered}
\]
For every original predicate in \(\Sigma\) and every graph predicate
associated with a function in \(\Sigma\), require congruence in all
coordinates.  For such a predicate \(H\) of arity \(r\geq1\), this is
\[
 \forall\bar x\,\bar y\,
 \left[
  \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{r}E(x_i,y_i)\right)
  \to\bigl(H(\bar x)\leftrightarrow H(\bar y)\bigr)
 \right].
\]
For arity zero, congruence is a tautology and is omitted.
Finally, for each \(m\)-ary function \(f\in\Sigma\), include
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\forall x_1\cdots x_m\,\exists z\,
                   G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,z),\\
 &\forall x_1\cdots x_m\,z\,w\,
 \bigl((G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,z)\land
        G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,w))\to E(z,w)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(m=0\), the first sentence is \(\exists z\,G_c(z)\), and the
second is uniqueness modulo \(E\) for that unary graph.
The equivalence and conjunction symbols in these axioms have their
ordinary definitions in the selected primitives.
Only \(E\), original predicates from \(\Sigma\), and graphs of
functions from \(\Sigma\) occur in \(\operatorname{Ax}_\Sigma\).

\paragraph{Terms and formulas.}
For a term \(t\), define a relational formula \(V_t(z)\), where the
output variable \(z\) is fresh for \(t\), by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 V_x(z)&=E(x,z),\\
 V_{f(t_1,\ldots,t_m)}(z)
   &=\exists z_1\cdots z_m
       \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}V_{t_i}(z_i)
                       \land G_f(z_1,\ldots,z_m,z)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
All auxiliary variables are distinct and fresh for the entire input
formula, and bound variables are renamed when necessary.
For a constant this gives \(V_c(z)=G_c(z)\).
The empty conjunction is \(\top\), and an empty existential block
does nothing.

The formula translation \((\cdot)^r\) fixes \(\bot\), commutes with
the Boolean connectives and quantifiers, and translates atoms by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (P(t_1,\ldots,t_m))^r
  &=\exists z_1\cdots z_m
       \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}V_{t_i}(z_i)
                       \land P(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\right),\\
 (t=u)^r
  &=\exists z\,w\,
       (V_t(z)\land V_u(w)\land E(z,w)).
\end{aligned}
\]
A nullary atom is unchanged.
Every introduced variable is bound.  No original symbol is replaced
by the graph of a different symbol, so the translation preserves
which original side owns each predicate, function, or constant.

\paragraph{The quotient truth lemma.}
Let \(N\) be a nonempty relational structure satisfying
\(\operatorname{Ax}_\Sigma\), with domain \(D\).
Write \([a]\) for the \(E^N\)-class of \(a\in D\), and let \(Q\)
have domain \(D/E^N\).
Interpret an original predicate by
\[
 P^Q([a_1],\ldots,[a_m])
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N\models P(a_1,\ldots,a_m).
\]
Its congruence axiom makes this independent of the representatives.
Interpret \(f^Q([a_1],\ldots,[a_m])\) as the unique class \([b]\)
such that \(N\models G_f(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b)\).
Totality supplies a class, uniqueness makes it unique, and input
congruence makes it independent of the representatives of the inputs.
For constants the same clauses give a unique output class.
Logical equality in \(Q\) is identity of equivalence classes.

If \(s\) is an assignment into \(D\), write \(\bar s(x)=[s(x)]\).
Induction on a term proves
\[
 N,s[z:=a]\models V_t(z)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [a]=t^Q(\bar s).
\]
For a variable this is exactly the interpretation of \(E\).
For a function term, witnesses to the translated subterms give their
correct argument classes by induction, so its graph atom gives the
stated value class.  Conversely, choose representatives of the finitely
many argument classes.  Their term formulas hold by induction.
Totality gives a graph output in the required value class, and
congruence in the output coordinate permits replacement by the
specified representative \(a\).  This supplies all existential witnesses.
The constant case uses the same totality, uniqueness, and output
congruence with no arguments.

Induction on formulas now gives
\[
 N,s\models C^r
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q,\bar s\models C.
\]
For an original predicate atom, the term lemma and predicate congruence
give both directions.  For equality, the term lemma identifies the
two value classes, and \(E\) says exactly that they agree.
Bottom and the Boolean connectives follow from their truth clauses.
For a quantifier, every value in \(D\) maps to an equivalence class,
and every class has a representative in \(D\).  Thus existential
witnesses lift and descend, and the universal quantifier ranges
over all classes exactly as required.  This proves the full truth lemma.

\paragraph{The interpolant uses only common symbols.}
Set \(\operatorname{Ax}_i=\operatorname{Ax}_{\Sigma_i}\).
We have the relational validity
\[
 \models(\operatorname{Ax}_1\land A^r)
                 \to(\operatorname{Ax}_2\to B^r).
\]
Indeed, a countermodel would satisfy both axiom conjunctions,
\(A^r\), and \(\neg B^r\).
Its quotient for \(\Sigma_1\cup\Sigma_2\) would satisfy
\(A\land\neg B\) by the truth lemma, contradicting the original
valid implication.
Apply the already proved relational case to these two sentences.
It gives a relational sentence \(J\) with
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\models(\operatorname{Ax}_1\land A^r)\to J,\\
 &\models J\to(\operatorname{Ax}_2\to B^r).
\end{aligned}
\]
Its predicate vocabulary is contained in the intersection of the
two translated vocabularies.  Hence it can contain \(E\), common
original predicates, and \(G_f\) only for a function or constant
\(f\) occurring in both original sentences.

Decode \(J\) into a first-order sentence \(\theta\) by the atomic
replacements
\[
 E(x,y)\mapsto x=y,\qquad
 G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,z)\mapsto f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=z,
\]
keeping original predicates and commuting with all logical operations.
For a constant the second replacement is \(G_c(z)\mapsto c=z\).
This introduces only common original symbols; equality is logical,
as permitted in the theorem.

For any original structure \(M\), its canonical relational expansion
\(M^r\) has the same domain, interprets \(E\) as actual equality,
and interprets each \(G_f\) as the graph of \(f^M\).
It satisfies both axiom conjunctions.
Its quotient is canonically isomorphic to \(M\), so the quotient
truth lemma yields \(M\models C\) iff \(M^r\models C^r\).
Also induction directly on \(J\) yields
\(M^r\models J\) iff \(M\models\theta\).
The first interpolant implication therefore gives
\(\models A\to\theta\); the second, since \(M^r\models
\operatorname{Ax}_2\), gives \(\models\theta\to B\).
This proves sentence interpolation in the general signature.

\paragraph{Free variables.}
Let now \(\varphi,\psi\) be formulas.
For each variable \(x\in\FV(\varphi)\cup\FV(\psi)\), choose a distinct
fresh constant symbol \(c_x\), and replace its free occurrences by
\(c_x\).  Let the resulting sentences be \(\varphi^c,\psi^c\).
Validity of \(\varphi\to\psi\) under every assignment implies
validity of \(\varphi^c\to\psi^c\) under every interpretation of the
new constants.
Sentence interpolation produces \(\theta^c\) with only common
symbols.  A constant \(c_x\) can therefore occur in it only when
\(x\in\FV(\varphi)\cap\FV(\psi)\).

Rename bound variables of \(\theta^c\) away from this finite set,
then replace each \(c_x\) by \(x\), including occurrences inside terms.
Call the result \(\theta\).
For any original structure and assignment \(s\), interpret
\(c_x\) as \(s(x)\).  Induction on terms and formulas identifies
the truth of \(\theta^c\) in this expansion with the truth of
\(\theta\) at \(s\), and likewise for the two input formulas.
The two sentence implications thus become
\(\models\varphi\to\theta\) and \(\models\theta\to\psi\).
The construction gives the asserted free-variable intersection.
Distinct new constant symbols were never required to denote
distinct elements, so this argument covers assignments with equal
values as well.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p7.interp.4}{thm:beth}{Beth definability}
\begin{proof}
Write \(L\) for the signature obtained by removing \(R\), and let
\(n\geq0\) be the arity of \(R\).
Thus \(T\subseteq\operatorname{Sent}(L\cup\{R\})\).
Choose a fresh \(n\)-ary predicate \(R'\), and let \(T'\) be obtained
by uniformly replacing \(R\) by \(R'\) in every sentence of \(T\).
All symbols of \(L\), including functions and constants, remain fixed.
Choose fresh distinct constant symbols \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\).
If \(n=0\), this list is empty.

\paragraph{One finite interpolation problem.}
The set of sentences
\[
 T\cup T'\cup\{R(\bar c),\neg R'(\bar c)\}
\]
is unsatisfiable.  Otherwise its model would give two expansions of
one \(L\)-reduct satisfying \(T\): the first uses its interpretation
of \(R\), and the second uses its interpretation of \(R'\) as \(R\).
Implicit definability makes these relations equal, contradicting the
two displayed literals.
Compactness, Theorem~\ref{thm:fol-compactness}, therefore supplies
finite \(\Delta,\Gamma\subseteq T\) for which
\[
 \Delta\cup\Gamma'\cup
       \{R(\bar c),\neg R'(\bar c)\}
\]
is unsatisfiable.  If a literal was absent from the initial finite
unsatisfiable subset, adding it preserves unsatisfiability.
The primes on \(\Gamma'\) denote the same uniform predicate renaming.
Set
\[
 A=\left(\bigwedge\Delta\right)\land R(\bar c),
 \qquad
 B=\left(\bigwedge\Gamma'\right)\to R'(\bar c),
\]
with empty conjunctions equal to \(\top\).
The finite unsatisfiability statement is exactly \(\models A\to B\).

Craig interpolation, Theorem~\ref{thm:craig-interpolation}, gives a
sentence \(J(\bar c)\) with
\[
 \models A\to J(\bar c),\qquad
 \models J(\bar c)\to B.
\]
Here the notation \(J(\bar c)\) names its possible parameter constants,
not free variables.
The predicate \(R\) occurs only on the first side, and \(R'\) only
on the second.  Neither can occur in \(J\).
Apart from the fresh constants, every nonlogical symbol in \(J\)
lies in \(L\), indeed in the intersection of the finite \(L\)-vocabularies
of the two conjunctions.
The two implications can be written
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\Delta\models R(\bar c)\to J(\bar c),\\
 &\Gamma'\models J(\bar c)\to R'(\bar c).
\end{aligned}
\]
Uniformly rename \(R'\) back to \(R\) in the second implication.
Since \(J\) contains neither predicate, it remains unchanged.
Thus, for the single finite set \(T_0=\Delta\cup\Gamma\subseteq T\),
\[
 T_0\models R(\bar c)\leftrightarrow J(\bar c).
\]

\paragraph{Removing the parameters.}
Take pairwise distinct variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\).
First rename the bound variables of \(J\) away from them, then
replace each fresh constant \(c_i\) by \(x_i\), including occurrences
inside compound terms.  Call the result \(\theta(\bar x)\).
It is an \(L\)-formula with no free variables outside \(\bar x\).
Its nonlogical vocabulary is finite, as every formula is finite.

Let \(M\models T_0\), and choose any tuple
\((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) from its domain.
Expand \(M\) by interpreting \(c_i\) as \(a_i\).
The constants do not occur in \(T_0\), so this expansion still
satisfies \(T_0\).  The last displayed consequence gives
\[
 R^M(a_1,\ldots,a_n)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 M,\bar x\mapsto\bar a\models\theta(\bar x),
\]
where the identification on the right follows by the ordinary
term and formula substitution induction.
Distinct constant symbols may denote the same element; no inequality
between tuple entries has been assumed.
Since the tuple was arbitrary,
\[
 T_0\models\forall\bar x\,
               (R(\bar x)\leftrightarrow\theta(\bar x)).
\]
First-order completeness, Theorem~\ref{thm:fol-completeness}, yields
the displayed derivation from \(T_0\), and therefore from \(T\).
The same finite support works for all models and all tuples:
\(\Delta,\Gamma\), and \(J\) were chosen before any model or assignment.

When \(n=0\), the argument uses no fresh constants or variables and
gives the sentence \(R\leftrightarrow\theta\) directly.
If \(T\) is inconsistent, compactness gives a finite inconsistent
subset and \(\theta=\bot\) also serves as an explicit definition.
The theorem makes no assumption that every \(L\)-structure has a
\(T\)-expansion; it compares those expansions that satisfy \(T\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p07-relative-proof-theoretic-ordinal}{A formula-class-relative proof-theoretic ordinal}
Fix a coding that effectively enumerates recursive binary relations
\(e\mapsto(D_e,\prec_e)\), where each \(D_e\) is a recursive subset of
\(\N\), and fix a class \(\mathcal C\) of formulas.  For a theory \(T\), one
standard first-order calibration is the supremum of
\(\operatorname{otp}(D_e,\prec_e)\) over those \(e\in\N\) for which
\((D_e,\prec_e)\) is externally a well-order and \(T\) proves every instance
of \(\mathcal C\)-transfinite induction along \(\prec_e\).
The index varies across the set whose supremum is taken; fixing one relation
and then reusing it in the set-builder would not define this calibration.  An
order type enters the set only after external well-foundedness of its coded
relation has been established.  This definition names a metalinguistic
calibration relative to the formula class, relation coding, and induction
reading; it is not an intrinsic ordinal object inside \(T\).  The
qualifications are nonredundant: consistency, reflection, provably total
functions, and provable well-foundedness can yield different comparisons.
The table below uses this distinction rather than an unqualified vertical-bar
notation for a theory; vertical bars are reserved for cardinality.
\index{proof-theoretic ordinal!relative calibration}
\index{transfinite induction!ordinal analysis}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p07-veblen-hierarchy}{Veblen hierarchy and \(\Gamma_0\)}
An ordinal function is \emph{normal} when it is strictly increasing and is
continuous at every nonzero limit.  Set
\(\operatorname{Veb}_0(\beta)=\omega^\beta\).  For \(\alpha>0\), let
\(\operatorname{Veb}_\alpha\) enumerate in increasing order the common fixed
points of all \(\operatorname{Veb}_\gamma\) with \(\gamma<\alpha\).  The
ordinal \(\Gamma_0\) is
the least positive \(\gamma\) satisfying
\(\operatorname{Veb}_\gamma(0)=\gamma\).

The locally defined symbol \(\operatorname{Veb}\) names this external
hierarchy of ordinal functions; it is distinct from the global formula
metavariables and is needed in the displayed definition of \(\Gamma_0\).
These clauses also define the one ordinal \(\Gamma_0\).  The hierarchy extends
the Cantor-normal-form vocabulary of Part~6 because
fixed points of earlier normal functions must themselves be enumerated.  The
distinction is used in the final row of
Table~\ref{tab:p07-ordinal-calibration}; no ordinal-analysis claim beyond
\(\Gamma_0\) is made here.
\index{Veblen hierarchy}
\index{Gamma-zero@\(\Gamma_0\)}
\end{hbdefinition}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p07-church-rosser}{proved=annex:p7.lambda.1}{Church--Rosser theorem}
If
\(M\longrightarrow_{\beta}^{*}N_1\) and
\(M\longrightarrow_{\beta}^{*}N_2\), then there is a term \(P\) such that
\(N_1\longrightarrow_{\beta}^{*}P\) and
\(N_2\longrightarrow_{\beta}^{*}P\).
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p7.lambda.1}{thm:p07-church-rosser}{Church--Rosser by parallel reduction}
\begin{proof}
All terms in Method~\ref{def:p07-parallel-reduction} are read modulo
alpha-equivalence.  First observe, by induction on a term, that
\(M\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}M\): use the variable clause at a variable and the
application and abstraction clauses at the two constructors.  The same
induction shows that complete development respects alpha-equivalence.  The
only nonliteral step is an abstraction: after replacing
\(\lambda y.P\) by \(\lambda z.P[z/y]\), with \(z\) fresh, the induction
hypothesis gives
\(\operatorname{dev}(P[z/y])=_{\alpha}
  \operatorname{dev}(P)[z/y]\).  Whether an application has an abstraction at
its head is unchanged by alpha-renaming, so the two application clauses of
\(\operatorname{dev}\) agree on alpha-equivalence classes.

We next prove the parallel-substitution lemma:
\[
 M\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}M',\quad
 N\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}N'
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 M[N/x]\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}M'[N'/x].                 \tag{1}
\]
Before the induction, alpha-rename every binder in the displayed parallel
derivation away from \(x\) and from the free variables of \(N,N'\); the first
paragraph shows that this changes neither hypothesis nor conclusion.  Induct on the displayed derivation of
\(M\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}M'\).  If \(M=x\), both sides of (1) are
\(N\) and \(N'\), so use the second hypothesis.  If \(M=y\ne x\), both
sides are \(y\), so use reflexivity.  The application case follows by applying
the induction hypotheses to the two subterms and then the application clause.
For an abstraction \(\lambda y.P\), freshness gives \(y\ne x\); apply the
induction hypothesis to \(P\) and use the abstraction clause.  In the beta
case write the source as \((\lambda y.P)Q\) and the target as
\(P'[Q'/y]\).  The induction hypotheses give
\(P[N/x]\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}P'[N'/x]\) for the body and the analogous
statement for the argument.  If the redex binder is \(y\), the beta clause
then has target
\(P'[N'/x][Q'[N'/x]/y]\), which is alpha-equal to
\((P'[Q'/y])[N'/x]\) because \(y\notin\FV(N')\).  This
composition-of-substitutions identity follows by induction on \(P'\),
alpha-renaming an abstraction binder fresh for all substituted terms; thus no
textual substitution or capture is used.

The development lemma is
\[
 M\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}P
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 P\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}\operatorname{dev}(M).          \tag{2}
\]
Induct on the parallel derivation.  The variable case is immediate.  The
abstraction case follows from the induction hypothesis and the abstraction
clause.  For an application-congruence conclusion
\(MN\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}M'N'\), use the two induction hypotheses.  If
\(M\) is not an abstraction, the application clause gives
\(M'N'\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}
  \operatorname{dev}(M)\operatorname{dev}(N)\), which is
\(\operatorname{dev}(MN)\).  If \(M=\lambda x.Q\), the induction hypotheses
give
\(M'=_{\alpha}\lambda x.Q'\) with
\(Q'\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}\operatorname{dev}(Q)\), and
\(N'\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}\operatorname{dev}(N)\); the beta clause therefore
gives
\[
 M'N'\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}
 \operatorname{dev}(Q)[\operatorname{dev}(N)/x]
 =\operatorname{dev}(MN).
\]
Finally, if the last rule is the parallel beta clause, its conclusion is
\(Q'[N'/x]\).  The induction hypotheses for the body and argument, followed
by (1), give
\[
 Q'[N'/x]\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}
 \operatorname{dev}(Q)[\operatorname{dev}(N)/x],
\]
again exactly the complete development of the source redex.  This exhausts
the four clauses and proves (2).

If
\(M\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}N_0\) and
\(M\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}N_1\), (2) supplies
\(N_i\mathrel{\mathsf{Par}}\operatorname{dev}(M)\) for both \(i\).
Thus one-step parallel reduction has the diamond property.

It remains to relate the auxiliary relation to ordinary beta reduction.  A
root beta contraction is a parallel beta step by reflexivity of the developed
body and argument; induction on a term context closes this fact under
application and abstraction.  Hence
\(\longrightarrow_\beta\subseteq\mathsf{Par}\).  Conversely, induction on a
parallel derivation sequentializes it.  The variable case takes no beta step;
the application and abstraction cases concatenate the finite reductions of
their subterms inside the corresponding contexts; and the parallel beta case
first reduces the body and argument inside
\((\lambda x.M)N\) to \((\lambda x.M')N'\) and then contracts the root redex
to \(M'[N'/x]\).  Therefore
\(\mathsf{Par}\subseteq\longrightarrow_\beta^{*}\), and the two relations
have the same reflexive--transitive closure.

For completeness, lift the one-step diamond to finite paths explicitly.  Given
paths of lengths \(m,n\) from one term, place them along the left and top edges
of an \(m\)-by-\(n\) grid.  Induct lexicographically on the cell coordinates.
At each cell the already constructed top and left edges are two parallel steps
with a common source; the diamond property supplies the bottom and right edges.
After finitely many cells, the lower-right corner is reachable from both path
endpoints.  Replacing each parallel edge by its finite beta simulation gives a
common beta reduct.  This is exactly the assertion of
Theorem~\ref{thm:p07-church-rosser}.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}
